narrative_purpose: Shows why planting saplings cannot replace old-growth structure: a usable vertebrate hollow emerges only through accumulated injury, fungal decay and insect excavation over centuries.
subject: The same eucalyptus trunk appears in four matched vertical cutaways across its life. The young trunk is solid with smooth bark. The next has a storm-broken branch stub admitting moisture and pale fungal threads. The third has dark softened heartwood riddled by insect galleries and a small cavity opening. The oldest has thick fissured bark and a deep dry hollow large enough for a possum and nesting bird, while the living sapwood forms a sound ring around it. The outer trunk diameter increases realistically at each stage.
scene: A quiet Australian woodland specimen sequence with the surrounding forest held soft and nearly identical so time is read from the wood rather than a changing landscape.
camera: Matched front-on trunk sections at the same viewing distance, interior exposed by a clean naturalist cutaway.
light: Cool forest shade and cyan fungal edges dominate; a restrained amber interior glow marks the final habitable cavity without turning it magical.
palette: Indigo understory, teal-grey bark and sapwood, cyan fungal threads, sparse amber inside the mature hollow.
style: Painterly dendrology and decay plate, botanically coherent and materially detailed.
detail_level: Crisp bark, branch scar, fungal front, galleries and final hollow; background foliage remains soft.
composition: Four trunks progress left to right from solid sapling to mature hollow-bearing veteran, aligned at the base. Leave dark strips beside the injury, decay front and final occupants framed by deep negative space.
consistency_notes: The hollow must develop from a natural branch injury through fungal and insect decay while living sapwood persists around it. Do not show a dead hollow log as the final stage.
negative_prompt: no text, no age numbers, no arrows, no carved doorway, no fantasy tree face, no photo, no CGI, no vector timeline
